# Preface.

## To the Gracious Reader:

The Publisher of this work has placed the present volume into my hands, having received a Latin manuscript in which various authors can be found who have written about the so-called <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>original: "Lapide Philosophorum"; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life</note>. He requested that I translate it from the Latin into the German language. I have very gladly complied with this request, since there are others who do not understand the Latin language yet are nonetheless <term>curious</term> <note>original: "curiös"; in this period, it refers to a person who is a "curioso," an intellectually inquisitive seeker of hidden or scientific knowledge</note> to have information on one thing or another. Indeed, there are many reasonable and clever people who nevertheless do not know the Latin language, seeing as languages are merely a <term>vehicle</term> <note>original: "Vehiculum"; a medium or tool used to transport meaning</note> to provide some report of this or that matter.

...added an epistle of my late brother, namely his **Judgment on the Allied Hermetic Duumvirs** <note>original: "Judicium de Duumviris Hermeticis Foederatis"; 'Duumvirs' refers to a pair of men holding joint office or authority, likely referring here to a specific pair of alchemical authors</note>, and their epistle **The Trumpeter** <note>original: "Buccinator"; a title often given to works that "proclaim" or "sound the trumpet" for a specific doctrine</note>, since such a thing is no longer easily obtainable; it has, however, been diligently translated from Latin into German. 

As for the present work, among these twelve ancient philosophers, one is clearer than the other, yet they agree fairly well on the primary Work. In several places, the work is described obscurely enough that one has good reason to read through it more than once with careful consideration; and it caused me no little trouble to extract the meaning in several places, especially where the scribe used few commas and other divisions, and also employed various unknown abbreviations, so that one sometimes did not know whether this or that turn of phrase belonged to what came before or after. This was particularly true where the old <term>monkish style</term> <note>original: "Mönchs-Stylus"; a term for medieval Scholastic or ecclesiastical Latin, which later scholars often found difficult or grammatically non-standard</note> was very prominent in the Latin manuscript; for example, using "It is unfolded" <note>original: "Explicet"; a common medieval manuscript term indicating the end of a roll or book</note> instead of "It is the end" <note>original: "Finis est"</note>, etc. Regarding this, the learned Reyher <note>likely referring to Samuel Reyher (1635–1714), a prominent polymath and professor known for his works on law, mathematics, and alchemy</note> is well able to provide sufficient information.

Regarding the works of the old philosophers <term>Philosophis|The "philosophers" or alchemists of antiquity whose writings formed the basis of the Hermetic tradition</term>, it is said: Nature and Art <note>In this context, "Art" refers to Alchemy—the human skill used to perfect or assist natural processes</note> must be together; without Art, Nature does not succeed, and without Nature, Art can begin nothing.

As noble as the magnet is, it costs very little and is easily obtained—namely, the magnet is available at all times. However, the solvent <term>Menstruum|A universal alchemical solvent believed to dissolve substances into their primary essence</term> can only be obtained at a certain time; and when one collects this doubled solvent <note>original: "Menstruum duplicatum"</note>, the process must be handled very cleanly; afterwards, it is kept for use. Gold is dissolved very quickly in this solvent, faster than in my other two. What further powers are within it, I shall investigate further, God willing <note>original: "g. G.", likely an abbreviation for "Gott gebe" (God grant) or "geliebt' Gott" (beloved God)</note>.

One can sometimes obtain much of this solvent, sometimes little, and sometimes none at all, which is why the time and hour must be well observed; otherwise, the Bird of Paradise <term>Paradies-Vogel|An alchemical metaphor for a volatile, spiritual substance or "spirit" that evaporates or escapes if the apparatus is not sealed or the timing is wrong</term> flies away until another Phoenix burns and a young one arises from it again: Therefore, let nothing be neglected.

After I, as a true philosopher <note>original: *Philosophus*</note>, rejected and cast aside various operations of Quicksilver <note>original: *Argenti viv.* (Argentum vivum), literally "living silver."</note>, I resolved to correctly name the true Philosopher’s Stone <note>original: *Lapidem Philosophor.*</note>, from which our true Quicksilver or Metal-Mercury <term>Queck-Metall|A term used by alchemists to distinguish their "philosophical" mercury from common quicksilver found in shops.</term> can be extracted, which in the end is converted into a true Medicine. # Of the Blessed Stone
<meta>catchword: a</meta>

This stone is now the blessed stone, the <term>Mineral Stone|Lapis mineralis; a name emphasizing that the stone originates from mineral substances rather than plants or animals</term>, brought forth from our <term>Quicksilver|Argentum vivum; literally "living silver," the alchemical name for Mercury</term>. It is sulfurous <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" refers to the active, combustible, and masculine principle within a substance, not just the yellow chemical element.</note> like other metals; it is equal to them in nature and complexion, and is a stone acceptable to the metals themselves. It is also joined with the metals because it is itself congealed and thickened from their very nature.

It is ripened and cooked halfway through its part, and in this respect, it is distinguished from common, <term>raw Quicksilver|Argento vivo crudo</term>. This is because its subtle moisture—or its <term>superfluity|superfluuum; the unnecessary or "excess" parts of a substance that must be purged</term>, its excessive essence—is raised and light, elevated from that same matter.

Its closer parts are large and coarse, and they hold those <term>moistures|humiditates; the liquid, feminine principle in alchemy</term>. When it is thickened in its specific form, it will be metallic, hard, and perfect, because its joining or <term>conjunction|Conjunction</term> occurs from and with a strong union with dryness <note>original: *ex forti unione cum sicco*; alchemists believed that the "dry" principle provided the "fixity" or hardness to a substance.</note>. These qualities are lacking in common quicksilver; therefore, it cannot mix, nor can it attach and <term>adhere|adhæriren</term> to the bodies <note>The "bodies" refers to the solid base metals, such as lead or tin, which the alchemist seeks to transform.</note> in their deep nature.

# Of the Blessed Stone
<meta>catchword: Stone</meta>

Regarding this Stone, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the father of alchemy.</note> and Aaron <note>Likely referring to a figure in alchemical literature often associated with early chemical processes.</note> say: Take a lovely, fresh herb—**the new honorary herb** <note>original: *herbam honorariam novam*; an alchemical metaphor for a specific mineral substance that "grows" in a particular way.</note>—which is found above the mountains; grind it immediately just as it is in its soil, and this is a **Body** <note>In alchemy, a "Body" (Corpus) refers to the solid, stable part of a substance that can withstand heat.</note> which endures the fire and is a beginning of the true **Philosopher's Stone** <note>original: *Lapid. Philosophorum*; the legendary substance capable of transmuting metals and healing the body.</note>.

It is therefore clear that common and crude <term>quicksilver|Queck-Metall; an old term for mercury</term> is not found above the mountains, but rather in the subterranean earth, running through the ground or the veins of the earth, **descending lower into the excavations** <note>original: *inferius descendens infossatis*</note> when one digs into the caverns.

It is impossible to make such a fixed Body out of it which might withstand the fire, as Ereberus <note>Likely a corruption of "Geber" (Jabir ibn Hayyan), the most influential medieval alchemical authority.</note> testifies, saying: **Quicksilver** <note>original: *Argentum vivum*</note> leaves behind—for many reasons—**its composite parts in a divided state** <note>original: *partes compositionis suæ esse divisas*</note>; it is probable, for many reasons, that its composite particles are divided, for the thing itself in its entirety <note>original: *ipsum totum*</note>, with its whole substance and essence, passes away in the fire and flees from it. Therefore it is evident that common quicksilver cannot be the Philosopher's Stone, as Alphidius <note>An alchemical authority, likely a Latinized Arabic author, frequently cited in the Middle Ages.</note> confirms, saying: Our work is a stone and not a stone; it is a stone in appearance and to the touch, but it is not a stone in its nature, nor is it compared with other stones—or rather, it is incomparable to them—of which Stone he says in his Testament: Our Stone...

### What is the Cause of Errors in This Art?

The cause of the error, through which most people err in our art, is that they do not take the true matter; therefore, Diomedes <note>original: *Dyamedes*; a philosopher cited in early alchemical compendiums.</note> says in the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba*; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts translated from Arabic.</note>: Honor that matter from which our art is made, for it comes from no other.

Alphidius <note>An Arabic alchemical authority frequently cited in medieval European texts.</note>: The Philosopher's Stone is composed of four natures; it is within such things and is formed therein, which thing is found in no other stone; therefore, our work cannot be made from any other matter.

Whatever it may be in the whole world, it is and becomes nothing except from our matter alone, and this is our proof <note>original: *approbatio*</note>.

# Of the Blessed Stone

This is the **rectification** <note>original: *Rectificatio*; the process of refining or purifying a substance through repeated cycles of distillation or sublimation.</note> of the **destruction** of the body, as has been said before.

### How our sublimation is called by the Philosophers by various unknown and obscure names.

This operation of sublimation is, therefore, the first rectification of our **Stone**, and it is unknown to many modern and new practitioners or laboratory workers <note>original: *Operatoribus* or *Laboranten*</note>. Consequently, they fall into error, especially because the **Philosophers** <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the lineage of historical alchemical masters.</note> have given it all sorts of names. For some call our sublimation a **dissolution**, others an **abluition** <note>A washing or cleansing process.</note>, and others a **distillation**.

The reason and intent of the **Philosophers** <note>original: *Philosophorum*</note> for giving such names is this: because a thing which is sublimated through fire must be melted before it rises from the fire; and because everything can be melted, they have also named sublimation a **dissolution into water** <note>original: *Dissolutionem in aqvam*</note>. The second reason is that everything which is sublimated and rises into the heights is consumed into a smoke, and the smoke or vapor is a water.

The third reason <note>original: *Ration*</note> why the Philosophers have called sublimation a "dissolution" is that by means of nature, the **matter** <note>original: *Materie*</note> is increased, thickened, and gathered together; the earthy and combustible particles with the subtle and watery...

It defines sublimation as a process of melting and vaporizing material to separate pure "watery" spirits from combustible "earthy" parts.</summary>

# Of the Blessed Stone

The operation called Expansion <note>Latin: *dilationem*; referring to the spreading out or rarefaction of a substance.</note>, rises in the form of a smoke into the top of the alembic <note>An alembic is the top cap of a distilling apparatus, used to catch and condense vapors.</note>. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> says of this: "The wind has carried it in its belly" <note>original Latin: *Ventus portavit in Ventre suo*. This is a famous line from the *Emerald Tablet*, the foundational text of Hermeticism.</note>, and with these words, he is referring to our distillation.

### Secondly, that our Sublimation has been called Destruction, Pulverization, Calcination, or Grinding by the Philosophers.

When the sublimation has occurred, there follows Destruction or Calcination, or Pulverization, or Grinding <note>Latin: *Destructio*, *Calcinatio*, *Pulverisatio*, or *Contritio*.</note>. This is as much as to say that something—specifically a "Body"—is converted or brought into <term>calx</term> <note>A fine powder or ash produced by burning a mineral or metal; in alchemy, this represents the "death" of the material before its rebirth.</note> by means of fire, as is very well known in Chemistry and Alchemy.

Our Sublimation happens for two reasons: (1.) Because through our distillation, destruction, or calcination, the aforementioned earthly and combustible particles are consolidated and broken <note>original: *consolidiret und frangiret*.</note> so that they may be better separated and refined; (2.) So that the subtle, tinting <term>anima</term> <note>Latin: soul; the vital essence or "tincture" of the substance.</note>—or Soul—can be extracted more easily and better from the destroyed and calcined Body. When this Soul is mixed with the Spirit, the true Elixir is prepared from it.

### Concerning the various colors which commonly appear in the **fixed Body**, and specifically through the **governance**, *Regimen*, of the fire.

It is well to note that in the **fixation** <note>original: "fixation"; the alchemical process of making a substance stable so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to heat.</note> different types of open fire are necessary. And within the **Matter** <note>original: "Materie"; the physical substance being worked on in the alchemical vessel.</note>, the different colors of the whole world appear, among which three in particular are the most prominent: namely, **Blackness, Whiteness, and Redness.** Many other different colors also appear as the **Matter** passes from one color into another and is **transmuted** <note>original: "transmutiret"; transformed from one state or substance into another.</note>, such as lemon-yellow. The **Philosophers** <note>original: "Philosophi"; a term used for alchemists and natural scientists of the past.</note> mention this color only briefly, as it is not stable—indeed, it is hardly seen or observed by the **practitioner** <note>original: "Laboranten"; the person performing the lab work.</note>.

Each of these principal colors shows that within four days, or slightly more, the lemon-yellow color reveals itself after the **Whiteness** and appears before the final **Redness**, provided there is a sufficient duration of time given to the **Matter**.

For this reason, some **Philosophers** have opined that the lemon-yellow color is the most significant. However, I have found in **my own practice** <note>original: "praxi mea"</note> that there are still only three principal colors, which I mentioned above. Therefore, in our **Work** <note>original: "Wercke"; the "Great Work" of alchemy, the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, I do not consider this lemon color to be sufficient <note>In this context, meaning "of primary importance" or "a defining stage".</note>, but rather the three colors named above.

Lucas <note>An unidentified alchemical author, possibly a pseudonym for a Greek or Arabic authority</note>: Our fire should be gentle for the Whiteness, until it is coagulated.

Hermogenes <note>Likely referring to the legendary Hermetic tradition</note>: While we cook our ore <term>æs</term> <note>original: *æs*; can refer to copper, bronze, or the "body" of the metallic matter</note>, it becomes water, and the more we cook it, the more it is inspissated <term>inspissated</term> <note>original: *inspissiret*; a process of thickening a liquid by boiling or evaporation</note>—that is, thickened.

Alcanus speaks: Why then do we divide our water? One part we cook, and one part we imbibe <term>imbibe</term> <note>original: *imbibiren*; the process of a dry solid slowly soaking up a liquid until it is saturated</note>, which part is called the Ferment <term>ferment</term> <note>original: *Fermentum*; a catalyst that triggers the final transformation of the alchemical matter</note>.

If you coagulate everything well in liquefaction <note>original: *liqvefactione*; the state of being dissolved or melted</note>, it becomes water; such we coagulate thereafter through cooking, and then the Redness <note>The *Rubedo*, the final successful stage of the Great Work</note> appears.

The Philosophers speak: You must and shall imbibe or soak your matter from the residue <note>original: *ex Residuo*</note> of the water, up to 7 ounces, or 14 loth <note>A traditional German unit of weight; 14 loth is equivalent to 7 ounces</note>, until it drinks its own water, and until the whole matter is dry and transformed into a dry earth. Amen.

### What now are the four first qualities?

The first four qualities are warm, dry, cold, and moist <note>original Latin: *calidum, siccum, frigidum, & humidum*</note>, and they are called the four first qualities for the reason that all four elements and temperaments <term>Complexiones</term> <note>The "complexions" or humors that determine a person's physical and mental constitution</note> are composed from them.

### Following this is what an element is, and how many elements there are?

There are four elements: Water, Air, Fire, and Earth. They are named Elements because every body <term>Corpus</term> in the world is composed of them, and from two qualities and no more. Thus, Fire consists of warm and dry; Air consists of warm and moist; Water consists of moist and cold; and Earth consists of cold and dry.

### Now follows which quality belongs to an element essentially, and which accidentally.

Heat is in Fire essentially <term>essentialiter</term> <note>an inherent, defining characteristic</note>, and dryness is there accidentally <term>accidentaliter</term> <note>a secondary characteristic that can change without changing the nature of the substance</note>. In the Air, however, the

### What then is an Elemented Thing <term>Elementatum</term>?

That is called an elemented thing which consists of more than two qualities and is composed of them; and in this, Elements and Elemented Things <note>original Latin: *Elementa & Elementata*</note> differ. 

### What is the Fifth Essence <term>Quinta Essentia</term>?

The Fifth Essence exists by itself <note>original Latin: *per se*</note> and differs from all Elements and Elemented Things in matter and form, as well as in power <note>original Latin: *in materia & forma, auch in potentia*</note>. It is subject to no decay <term>Corruption</term> <note>the process of breaking down or rotting</note> and is for that reason called the Fifth Essence, because it is extracted from all elements. Within it, there is no essential movement <note>original Latin: *essentialis motio*</note> as there is in other elemented bodies <note>original Latin: *elementatis corporibus*</note>.

The first cause is the movement of the earth and the influence of the heavens. The accidental causes <note>original Latin: *Causa accidentalis*</note> are Sulfur, Air, and Quicksilver <note>original Latin: *Sulphur, Aër, & arg. Viv.*</note>—warm, dry, earthy, fiery, or hot—and their Sulfur. The joined causes <note>original Latin: *Causæ adjunctæ*</note> are the sulfurous vapor and quicksilver, because it is hidden in a destroyed place <note>original Latin: *in loco destructo*</note> and is generated within itself.

### What then is called *Living Silver* in our Art?

Living Silver <note>original: *Argentum vivum*</note> is named Common Salt <note>original: *Sal commune*</note> <note>In alchemy, "Common Salt" rarely refers to table salt, but rather a "philosophical salt" or a purified mineral base necessary for the work.</note>. Rosarius <note>likely the author of the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical text</note> speaks thus: Common Salt dissolves gold and silver, and increases the redness in gold and the whiteness in silver; it changes them from corporeality into spirituality, and with it, the Bodies <note>original: *Corpora*</note> are calcined <term>Calcination</term> <note>the process of heating a substance until it is reduced to a fine powder or ash, the first step in the Great Work</note>.

Haimo <note>a medieval philosopher-monk often cited in alchemical compendiums</note>, a philosopher, says because of this: If God had not created this salt, no one could make our elixir, and all the work of the alchemists would be in vain.

Parmenides in the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: He who works without this salt accomplishes nothing; this salt consumes and eats away the blackness, drives away the foul smell, and dissolves everything and cleanses it. In our Art, no one can perform anything useful without this salt.

### It follows: from what things is the *Philosopher’s Stone* prepared?

To this, Petrus de Solento <note>an alchemical authority often cited in medieval and Renaissance collections</note> answers, saying: Our stone is called a stone because it has within itself a Soul <note>original: *Animam*</note>, a Spirit <note>original: *Spiritum*</note>, and a Body <note>original: *Corpus*</note>; all people possess this stone, both rich and poor, in imperfect bodies and perfect ones; without this stone, man cannot live.

Our stone grows between two mountains; Thus says Petrus de Solento: Go to the highest mountains in India, and take from them good stones. The mountains are the highest metals <note>original: *Metalla*</note>, that is, the most perfect <note>Alchemists often used "India" as a metaphor for a distant, exotic land of spiritual riches, while "mountains" represented the most noble metals, Gold and Silver, from which the "stones" or seeds of the Work were derived.</note>.

### Our Stone is called *Animated*.

Our Stone <note>original: *Lapis*</note> is called Animated <note>original: *Animatus*</note>; Thus says Petrus de Solento <note>a medieval alchemical authority often cited in collections like the *Theatrum Chemicum*</note>: Because it has within itself Body, Spirit, and Soul <note>original: *Corpus, Spiritum und Animam*</note>. [...let this] be his salvation; since I now well understand his meaning and everything he has said, I now ask: is <term>sublimation <note>A process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condensed back into a solid; in alchemy, this often symbolized the purification of the spirit from the body.</note></term> also necessary in this work, as all <term>sublimators <note>original: *Sublimatores*; those who focus on the repetitive distillation or rising of chemical vapors.</note></term> are accustomed to do?

My son, note that our sublimation is an elevation of the non-volatile parts from their <term>fixed parts <note>original: *fixen Theilen*; "fixed" substances are those that can withstand fire without evaporating.</note></term>; the non-fixed parts are brought on high, etc., and indeed through smoke and wind. We desire that both should be <term>fixed <note>original: *figiret*; the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</note></term> together, so that they may more easily become fluid. In this way, you shall now understand our sublimation.

The non-fixed parts are brought upward, etc., specifically through "smoke and wind." We desire that both be <term>fixed <note>original: *figiret*; to make a volatile or "spiritual" substance stable and solid so it can withstand heat.</note></term> together, so that they may more easily become fluid. In this way, you will now understand our sublimation.

# ...of the Wise.

Therefore, because the metals are born in the earth and come forth from it, they also grow and multiply <term>infinitely: without end or limit</term> <note>original: "in infinitum"</note>, which demonstrates that this possibility exists.

But the <term>metals: the various metallic elements</term> <note>original: "Metalla"</note> must first be <term>reduced: returned to a liquid or primal state</term> <note>original: "reduciret"</note> into the <term>first matter: the raw, undifferentiated substance from which all things originate</term> <note>original: "primam materiam"</note>, so that <term>generation: the act of creation or birth</term> <note>original: "generatio"</note> and multiplication can happen in and upon them, as has already been mentioned and explained above.

It is very beautiful and wonderful that in the melting of all things there is an <term>alteration: a fundamental change in nature or state</term> <note>original: "Alteration"</note>. One must bring it to the point where the <term>bodies: the solid physical substances</term> <note>original: "Corpora"</note>, <term>by liquefying: through the process of melting into liquid</term> <note>original: "liquefaciendo"</note>, become a water; this water is called by the <term>Philosophers: the alchemists and natural scientists of the era</term> <note>original: "Philosophis"</note> the <term>Water of Wisdom: a symbolic name for the universal solvent or purified mercurial liquid</term> <note>original: "Aqua sapientiæ"</note>. <term>Borax: a mineral salt often used as a flux in soldering and chemistry</term> <note>original: "Borrax"</note> dissolves all bodies; however, the work cannot happen without a <term>ferment: an agent that triggers a transformation, similar to how yeast works in bread</term> <note>original: "Ferment"</note>. The Sun <note>original: "Sol"</note>, which is Gold, is the king and head of all metals and stones, and neither earth, water, air, nor fire can corrupt it.

It is purified <note>original: "rectificiret"</note> and moistened <note>original: "humectiret"</note> by the process; it does not decrease, nor does sulfur burn it away.

Gold retains every body <note>original: "Corpus"</note> at the same time; nothing is <term>improved: raised to a higher quality or purity</term> <note>original: "meliorirt"</note> or completed <note>original: "complirt"</note> without it.

From the Gold comes the <term>ferment: the catalyst for change</term> <note>original: "Fermentum"</note> itself. It is the key to all secrets and is like the <term>rennet: the substance used to curdle milk into cheese</term> <note>original: "Coagulum"</note> in milk. And this is the Silver, which employs <note>original: "adhibiret"</note> the bodies.

### Of the Blessed Stone

<term>The Test: a process of trial or validation</term> <note>original: "Probatio, oder die Probation"</note> is when the <term>Spirits: the volatile, gaseous aspects of a substance</term> <note>original: "Spiritus"</note> and <term>Bodies: the solid, physical matter</term> <note>original: "Corpora"</note> unite, or are made to unite, so that they may prove their powers; for otherwise, this will not happen. The <term>Accidental Properties: external qualities like color or smell that are not part of the core essence</term> <note>original: "Accidentia"</note> cannot show their characteristics <note>original: "nisi fuerint Substantiis secreta"</note> unless they have been separated from the primary substances.

Likewise, those stones which do not endure in the fire cannot show their <term>virtues: the inherent powers or medicinal properties</term> <note>original: "virtutes"</note>, unless they are <term>married to fixed things: permanently joined to substances that do not evaporate in heat</term> <note>original: "fixis maritati"</note> (linked, overlaid, or bound); such stones do not accept one another unless they are both pure. For the Body does not <term>receive: take in or absorb</term> <note>original: "recipiret"</note> the Spirit, <note>original: "& e contrario"</note> and vice versa; that which has become spiritual does not become physical/corporeal unless it is perfectly cleansed of all impurity. At that point, the Bodies are <term>joined: united or married</term> <note>original: "jungiret"</note> by the Spirits during the <term>examination: the trial by fire</term> <note>original: "examine"</note>, and the Spirits are <term>bound: fixed so they no longer fly away</term> <note>original: "ligiret"</note> over the fire. Thus they reach <note>original: "ad fixionem & fusionem"</note> fixation and fusion without smoking; then all that is <term>subtle: refined and penetrating</term> <note>original: "subtile"</note> will overcome and penetrate every solid thing, as <term>Hermes: Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</term> <note>original: "Hermes"</note> says.

*Note*, that all Bodies can be <term>converted: transformed in nature</term> <note>original: "vertiret"</note> into <term>Quicksilver: mercury, often considered the "mother" of all metals</term> <note>original: "Argentum vivum"</note>; likewise, Quicksilver can be extracted from all Bodies. The confirmation of what was said before is to be proven by authority.

*Note*, that the <term>Everlasting Water: a symbolic term for a stable, non-evaporating alchemical liquid</term> <note>original: "immerwährende Wasser"</note> <term>coagulates: solidifies or thickens</term> <note>original: "coaguliret"</note> the Quicksilver. <note>original: "Aqua perennis"</note> Everlasting Water is a Body <term>dissolved: broken down into liquid state</term> <note>original: "solutum"</note> in Quicksilver, Spirit, and Soul.

### What is the fourth order?

Now place this whole mass—namely, the blackness that has been turned into whiteness—along with the clear **mercury** <term>mercury: here referring to the purified alchemical spirit, often called "mercury of the sages"</term> into a glass flask with a distilling head <note>original: "Helm"</note>. Apply a strong fire, and the middle part, bright and clear, will rise and be distilled; the blackness that has turned white will remain below, **calcined** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a dry powder</term>, and it will be of the nature of fire. Do this just as you did at first.

### What shall be the fifth order?

Afterward, take from the upper part—from the **ferment** <term>ferment: a substance, like gold or silver, used to "leaven" or transform the alchemical base into a noble metal</term> of the gold or silver—with respect to the earth which remained **at the bottom** <note>original: "in fundo"</note> and which has been well purified. Let **fire and soul** <note>original: "ignis & anima"</note> be added to it, and in such a manner **conjoin** <note>original: "conjungire"</note> it with the **quicksilver** <note>original: "Arg. viv." / "Argentum vivum"</note>. Wash it and **dissolve** <note>original: "solvire"</note> it in a glass flask; take away the blackness, **whiten** <note>original: "dealbire"</note> it, and **distill through an alembic** <term>alembic: a classic distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling vessel and a cooling cap to collect vapors</term> as before, in the same manner and fashion; **proceed in all things thus** <note>original: "per omnia sic procedas"</note>.

After the **decoctions** <term>decoction: a method of boiling a substance to extract its essence</term> are mixed, the colors will change in many different ways, but do not worry much about that; rather, **continue** your **decoction** and **imbibition** for so long until everything has been brought into one **body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note>. ### What is the seventh order?

The seventh order is the end of the Work <note>The Great Work, or "Magnum Opus," the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>; then you may increase the fire until it pleases the **Son** <term>the Son: a symbolic name for the evolving alchemical substance, often associated with the Red King or the Stone itself</term> himself to taste of the **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio"</note> as much as he desires, and so the Work is continued until you reach the **augmentation** <term>augmentation: the process of increasing the power, weight, or medicinal virtue of the alchemical stone</term>.

Afterward, when it has been augmented, you will arrive through the fire at a point where you see and obtain the **redness**, which looks like a **pomegranate syrup** <note>This signifies the "rubedo" or the final red stage of the process, indicating the perfection of the Stone.</note>; then you have the **crowned King**, whom you should heed and honor, and then he will in turn honor and heed you. Amen.

### What is the eighth order?

Afterward, you can augment this, as the philosophers say, and indeed **infinitely** <note>original: "in infinitum"</note>; nourish him with his own **milk** <note>Alchemical "milk" usually refers to the white mercurial liquid used to "feed" and grow the stone.</note> until he arrives at his first fire, which is very gentle, if God so wills—Who is to be praised for eternity, and to Whom thanks be given. Note that there are two **superior ferments** <note>original: "superiora fermenta"</note>, namely gold and silver, and you may take of them as much as you please.

### *TREATISE ON ALCHEMY.*

Now follows a very useful treatise on this art of *Alchemy*, which is divided into 18 chapters;

#### Its
#### First Chapter

->Deals with the fact that Mercury is the root, or *Radix*, of all things.<-

Mercury is the root of all things, *and he alone is to be restored* <note>original: *& ipse solus est reparandus*</note>, and from him comes a good binding and a strong *impression* <term>impression: the act of "imprinting" or fixing specific qualities or virtues onto a substance</term> and strength.

For it is itself the metal which holds within itself everything that we require for our *Mastery* <term>Mastery: also known as the *Magisterium*, this refers to the completion of the Great Work or the creation of the Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>original: *Magisterio*</note>. For one must *consider* <note>original: *consideriren*</note> how everything belongs to the work lies hidden within it, from the beginning until the end.

No other *simple element* <note>original: *Elementum simplex*</note> is more useful than this, for everything is purified through it; so that, when the purification has occurred and the impurity is cast away, the *operation* <note>original: *Operation*</note> may proceed all the more properly.

Insofar as a complete and *full preparation* <note>original: *complete Præparation*</note> goes before, it must necessarily follow that a complete and *perfect* <note>original: *perfecte*</note> fulfillment must also occur. And this is its entire *preparation* <note>original: *Præparation*</note>: namely, its *reduction* <term>reduction: the process of bringing a substance back to its original or essential state, often through liquefaction</term> <note>original: *Reduction*</note> to the nature of fire, to *dissolve* <note>original: *resolviren*</note> it into water.

## The Second Chapter.
->What Nature performs and does, and<-
->what Art performs and achieves,<-
->*according to Margarita*.<- <note>original: *secundum Margaritam*; a reference to the famous 14th-century alchemical text *Pretiosa Margarita Novella* (The Precious New Pearl) by Petrus Bonus.</note>

It is Nature that cooks, <term>digests</term> <note>a process of slow, gentle heating intended to mature or "ripen" a substance</note>, raises up, retains, sustains, seeks by boiling <note>original: *qvæ decoqvendo appetit*</note>, casts out, expels <note>original: *expellit*</note>, mixes, corrupts <note>original: *corrumpiret*; in alchemical theory, "corruption" is the necessary stage of decomposition before a new form can emerge</note>, begets, designs, prepares, forms, and gives shape <note>original: *informiret*</note> to the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term> <note>original: *Lapidem Philosophorum*</note>.

But <term>Art</term> <note>original: *Ars*; the skill, tools, and labor of the human alchemist</note> does not beget or destroy, nor does it design or prepare—it does not generate, nor corrupt, nor give form <note>original: *non generat, nec corrumpit, nec informat*</note>—rather, Art can do nothing else than offer a hand to Nature in this entire Work, and to stand by and serve working Nature.

Nature alone can perform nothing of the sort by herself, unless Art serves her; thus Nature and Art must be together. Nature works, and Art serves.

Therefore, if Nature is good, it is good; but where she is evil and bad, it is also bad; thus, if nature is good, it is well; if bad, it is bad <note>original: *Natura ideò si bona, benè, si mala, malè*</note>.

<term>Rhasis</term> <note>the Latinized name for Abu Bakr al-Razi, a famous 9th-century Persian alchemist and physician</note>: Mercury <note>original: *Mercurius*</note> is the root of every thing, and it must be prepared, and from it comes a good <term>Tincture</term> <note>a potent alchemical liquid or essence capable of transforming or "dyeing" metals</note>, which is strong and significant.

Without money, he can also begin nothing; for although the costs are not excessively great, everything still costs money. Most importantly, during the elaboration of such a work, he must be able to support himself, for he must generally direct his thoughts upon it and leave other matters aside. Materials, vessels, furnaces, coals, instruments, etc., must also be of good quality and close at hand.

# The Tenth Chapter
## Concerning the Distinction between Common Sulfur, [Sulfur] of the Art, and the Radical [Sulfur].

**W**hen we can obtain a **perfect body** <note>original: *perfect Corpus*; a substance that has reached its highest metallic or chemical state</note> from the purest **Mercury**, combined with a red sulfur, we should **choose** <note>original: *eligiren*</note> it for the red and white **Elixir** <note>the two stages of the Philosopher’s Stone: the white for turning metals to silver, and the red for gold</note>. And although Nature accomplishes much, she does not know how to purify correctly, as she works simply upon that which she has with and within herself.

However, there is a twofold **sulfurousness** <note>original: *sulphureitas*; the active, combustible, or "fiery" principle in alchemy</note> in the **bodies**: one is in **Mercury** and is enclosed within its solid **substance**. Therefore, this **Sulfur** is of such a kind that it completes and forms itself.

can bring it about so that the total of the <term>fixed</term> <note>original: des Fixi; referring to a substance that withstands the heat of the fire without evaporating</note> exceeds the total of the <term>volatile</term> <note>original: Summam volatilem; referring to a substance that easily evaporates or turns to smoke</note>, it occurs through the composition of simple elements <note>original: per compositionem simplicium elementorum</note>, and not otherwise; and this is the power of alchemy, and this is the strength of alchemy <note>original: & hæc est fortitudo Alchymiæ</note>.

Take the following parable: just as a human being is brought to completion from the beginning of conception, and becomes more perfect, and continues so until the time of birth, and at the time of their complete birth is perfect—yet if the human does not come out of the mother's womb and is born at the right time, they suffocate and die.

In the same way, when our stone arises, it is perfect in itself, yet the <term>tincture</term> <note>the concentrated essence or "dye" that gives the stone its power to transform metals</note> is missing, as is the stable formation, and likewise the <term>matrimonial union</term> <note>original: conjunctio matrimonialis; the chemical joining of opposing elements, often metaphorically described as the marriage of a King and Queen</note>; it therefore requires an artist who extracts <note>original: extrahiret</note> it, and then it will immediately appear perfect.

Now that we have noted everything that belongs to the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> and to nature, set your hands to this work.

But if you do not know or do not wish to know the truth of nature, do not approach this place, as it is very harmful.

One must have patience until the lilies emerge so that they can be plucked, and one must wait until the whiteness, or <term>whitening</term> <note>original: Dealbatio; also known as the "albedo" stage, where the matter is purified into a white state</note>, appears, which is the beginning and foundation of the work; the redness, however, is the <term>perfection</term> <note>original: Perfectio; the final "rubedo" stage where the stone achieves its full power</note>.

## The Thirteenth Chapter.
### How a Twofold Operation is Necessary in This Art.

Two kinds of operation are necessary in this art: namely, the <term>operation of the hands</term> <note>manual labor and the physical manipulation of the apparatus</note> and the <term>operation of diligent observation</term> or gazing with the eyes. The operation of the hands is used to take away what is superfluous, because nature works constantly and without ceasing throughout the entire time of <term>digestion</term> <note>the slow heating of a substance to mature it</note> by the <term>fire of sublimation</term> <note>original: ignem sublimationis; the process of vaporizing a solid and recollecting it as a purified form</note>. The artist must assist nature while she works alone; for even if nature herself casts out, throws off, or separates something superfluous, she cannot do it by herself unless she is assisted and helped. Indeed, she cannot take it away or remove it entirely; rather, the artist alone must perform this task.

> Socrates: Diligently seek the coldness of the <term>Moon</term> <note>original: Monden / Luna; in alchemy, this refers to the cool, silver-like, or feminine principle of the matter</note>; through this, you will afterwards also find the heat of the <term>Sun</term> <note>original: Sonnen / Sol; the hot, gold-like, or masculine principle</note>. Use your hands in this work so that everything superfluous and harmful may be removed. How necessary sight is will also be realized in this work—at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end—during the <term>decoction</term> <note>the process of boiling or heating a substance in a liquid</note> and sublimation, etc. And when all the <term>superfluous matter</term> <note>original: superflua; the dross or "dead" parts of the material that must be purged</note> is taken away, the artist will look upon the wonderful whiteness <note>The Albedo, or "White Stage," which signals that the matter has been purified</note> with astonishment.

One will find that which makes us rejoice in the work; for then, when the Moon is <term>chilled</term> <note>original: infrigidirt; cooled down</note>, the Sun is hidden in her innermost part, and the rising is <term>joined</term> <note>original: conjungiret</note> with the setting.

<summary>This chapter explains that the alchemist must use both manual labor to remove impurities and careful observation to monitor the transformation of the matter. It emphasizes the artist's role as a "helper of nature" in achieving the stage of the "wonderful whiteness."</summary>

...and the **Center of the Earth**, and the spiritual with the corporal <note>the joining of the intangible spirit and the physical matter</note>, as the Ancients have taught.

Know that you cannot dye into the **Purple color** <note>original: Purpur-Farbe; representing the final stage of the "Great Work," also known as the Rubedo</note> until you have first reached the **Whiteness** <note>original: Weiſſe; the Albedo stage, representing purification</note>. You should also know that while whatever evaporates is indeed processed during the operation, you have erred in the heat <note>too much evaporation suggests the fire was too intense, potentially damaging the matter</note>.

**Cool it down, therefore** <note>original: Infrigida ergò ipſum</note>; bring it then to the cold, and then that which is hidden will become manifest and will show itself in the cold.

And this **cooling** <note>original: infrigidation</note> happens in such a way that no further operation of the hands is necessary (namely, to remove the remaining unnecessary parts), for here, no more manual labor is required, because it is the end of the work.

**Pythagoras:** You should know that it makes many colors appear; it is as if he wanted to say: we need fire no longer, but rather through **cooling** <note>original: frigidando</note> we join the **spirits** and **bodies** <note>original: Spiritus und Corpora; combining volatile vapors with solid materials</note> together.

The first operation happens with the hands, which is the first degree, and it occurs **through sublimation and cleansing** <note>original: per ſublimationem & mundationem; the act of vaporizing a substance to purify it from dross</note>.

The other operation, however, happens in stillness and without labor, and is the second degree of the work, which occurs through **fixation** <note>original: fixion; the process of making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated</note> and the remaining of that which has been sublimated and cleansed, because the **active principle** <note>original: Agens</note>, once it has introduced the **form** <note>original: formam; the essential nature or identity of the new substance</note>, brings the work to its conclusion, rests, and takes delight.

## The Fourteenth Chapter,
### Concerning the Opinions on the Operations of the Stone, according to Pythagoras.

Our stone kills with its own projectile, it **dissolves** <note>original: *solviret*; the process of turning a solid into a liquid state</note> itself, it **calcinates** <note>original: *calciniret*; reducing a substance to a powder through heat</note> etc. itself in one day, or even in a shorter time; the Stone of the Sages must be made from **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurio*; quicksilver, seen here as the primary substance of the work</note> alone, **through Alchemy** <note>original: *per Alchymiam*</note>.

Yet, **Mercury** is of no value on its own; however, when it is **mortified** <note>original: *mortificiret*; the alchemical "death" or breakdown of a substance's initial form</note> with the hidden **Body** <note>original: *Corpore*</note>, it is then permanently retained with the same.

And because its **Body** is of the nature of Gold, of the **Sun** <note>original: *Solis*; the sun is the traditional planetary symbol for gold</note>, it is necessary that it be brought entirely to the nature of gold, and thus the entire work is brought into Gold; when the artist clearly beholds the **Soul** <note>original: *Animam*</note> beautiful, white, and bright, he should immediately **conjoin** <note>original: *conjungiren*; to unite or marry</note> it with the **Body**.

The **Soul** cannot be preserved without the **Body**, etc., and such joining and unification is the end of the work; although in truth and reality the stone itself, for its own sake, and concerning that which pertains to the **Soul, Body, and Spirit** <note>original: *Animam, Corpus & Spiritum*</note>, is always one and the same **in reality** <note>original: *secundum rem*</note>, yet one says—according to the various **reasonings** <note>original: *Rationibus*</note> and **intentions** <note>original: *Intentionibus*</note> of the **Philosophers** <note>the term "Philosophers" usually refers to historical alchemists</note>—that it is now this, then something else.

<meta>catchword: Sols (Sun's/Gold's)</meta>

<summary>This page outlines the self-contained nature of the alchemical stone, which dissolves and perfects itself, emphasizing that Mercury must be united with a "Body" of gold to reach the final goal. It identifies the unification of Soul, Body, and Spirit as the completion of the Great Work, noting that while these are distinct concepts to the philosophers, they are one in the physical Stone.</summary>

# The Fifteenth Chapter,

->In which is contained what the white gold is,<-
->according to the opinion of Rosinus.<- <note>Rosinus is the Latinized name often attributed to the 4th-century Egyptian-Greek alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis.</note>

If you do not add gold to gold, you will have nothing but a white gold; and the **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*; the transformative fluid or "quicksilver" of the alchemists</note>, which is neither sick nor healthy, finally reaches the perfection of gold. It is the same things that **whiten** <note>original: *dealbiren*; the *albedo* stage</note> and **redden** <note>original: *rubificiren*; the *rubedo* or final stage</note>, both internally and externally.

And because this entire **Body** <note>original: *Corpus*</note> and **Soul** <note>original: *Anima*</note> are united through the **Spirit** <note>original: *Spiritum*</note>, it is solely of the nature of Gold, even though at the end of the first **stage** <note>original: *Gradus*</note> it becomes white because of the nature of Silver. However, because the Gold is hidden there and thus dominates it by being a **Ferment** <note>original: *Fermentum*; a substance that "leavens" or transforms the whole mass</note>, it makes such a mass red in the second stage, in **the most proximate potential** <note>original: *potentia propinquissima*; a philosophical term meaning the matter is on the very verge of changing</note>.

But in the third stage, the **Ferment** rules in **actuality** <note>original: *Actu*</note>, and **converts by its power** <note>original: *convertit potentia*</note> that mass into a true redness, into a **true, actual redness** <note>original: *veram rubedinem actualem*</note>.

From which it is clear that the artist must always be vigilant when he is engaged in this work. Now, when he has come to the **first stage** <note>original: *ad gradum primum*</note>, let him stay there for a while, **because the Will completes the second stage and joins it to the first** <note>original: *qvia Voluntas perficit secundum gradum, & conjungit primo*</note>, and thus he has no need of repetition, just as in the boiling of honey and soap <note>This comparison suggests that once the chemical reaction reaches a certain point, it sustains itself until finished, like the thickening of syrup or soap-making.</note>.

## The Fourteenth Chapter,
### Regarding the Opinions on the Operations of the Stone, according to Pythagoras. <note>Pythagoras was revered by medieval alchemists not just as a mathematician, but as a master of cosmic harmony and the transformation of elements.</note>

Our stone kills with its own projectile, **dissolves** <note>original: *solviret*; the process of turning a solid into a liquid state</note> itself, **calcines** <note>original: *calciniret*; the reduction of a substance to a fine powder through heat</note> itself, and so forth, in a single day or even in a shorter time. The **Philosopher's Stone** <note>original: *Weisen-Stein*</note> must be made from **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurio*</note> alone, through the art of alchemy.

Yet, Mercury is of no value on its own; however, when it is **mortified** <note>original: *mortificiret*; a term for "killing" or fixing a volatile substance so it no longer evaporates</note> with the hidden **Body** <note>original: *Corpore*</note>, it is permanently retained within it.

And because its Body is by nature of Gold—of the **Sun** <note>original: *Solis*</note>—it is necessary that it be brought entirely to the nature of gold, and thus the whole work is transformed into gold. When the artist clearly beholds the **Soul** <note>original: *Animam*</note> as beautiful, white, and bright, he should immediately unite it with the Body.

The Soul cannot be preserved without the Body, and so forth; and such a joining and union is the end of the work. Although, in deed and truth, the Stone itself—in its own right and concerning its Soul, Body, and **Spirit** <note>original: *Spiritum*</note>—is always one and the same thing **according to the matter** <note>original: *secundum rem*</note>; nevertheless, according to the various **reasonings** <note>original: *Rationibus*</note> and **intentions** <note>original: *Intentionibus*</note> of the **philosophers** <note>original: *Philosophorum*</note>, one says that it is sometimes this, and sometimes something else.

# The Fifteenth Chapter,
## Wherein is contained what white gold is, according to the opinion of **Rosinus** <note>Rosinus is a Latinized name typically referring to Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist whose writings were foundational to the medieval tradition.</note>.

If you do not add gold to gold, you will have nothing but a white gold, and the **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*; regarded here as the "spirit" or living essence of the metal</note>, which is neither sick nor healthy, finally reaches the perfection of gold. It is the same things that **whiten** <note>original: *dealbiren*</note> and **redden** <note>original: *rubiciren*</note>, both internally and externally.

And because this entire **Body** <note>original: *Corpus*</note> and **Soul** <note>original: *Anima*</note> are united through the **Spirit** <note>original: *Spiritum*</note>, it is purely of the nature of gold, even if it becomes white at the end of the **first degree** <note>original: *Gradus*; a specific stage of heating or refinement</note> due to the nature of silver. However, because the gold is hidden within it and thus dominates it by acting as a **Ferment** <note>original: *Fermentum*; a substance, like yeast, that has the power to transform a larger mass into its own nature</note>, it makes such a **mass** <note>original: *Massam*</note> red in the second degree, **in its nearest potential** <note>original: *in potentia propinquissima*</note>.

But in the third degree, the **Ferment rules in Actuality** <note>original: *Fermentum in Actu*</note>, and **converts by its power** <note>original: *& convertit potentia*</note> that mass into a true redness, **into a true, actual redness** <note>original: *in veram rubedinem actualem*</note>.

From this it is evident that the artist must always be vigilant when engaged in this work. When he has reached the **first degree** <note>original: *ad gradum primum*</note>, he should stay there for a while, **because the Will perfects the second degree and joins it to the first** <note>original: *quia Voluntas perficit secundum gradum, & conjungit primo*</note>, and thus he does not need repetition, just as in the boiling of honey and soap. <note>This comparison suggests that once a chemical reaction reaches a certain point of "thickening" or "purity," it continues naturally to the next stage through steady heat without needing to start over.</note>

## The Sixteenth Chapter,

### Containing when the Union <term>Conjunction</term> should happen.

We say for certain that Nature governs this work of art through boiling <term>per decoctionem</term>, and indeed in its own fire and its own vessel, until the end of the work, and beyond <note>original: *& ultra*</note>.

But one wishes and should govern Nature, and as it were measure or weigh her at the end of the work, so that it does not rise beyond measure; for this matter requires the Union <term>Conjunction</term> and its Form, which is the Leaven <term>Fermentum</term> <note>In alchemy, the "ferment" is the substance that triggers the transformation of the base matter into the "gold" of the Philosopher's Stone, much like yeast transforms dough.</note>. This Leaven indeed lies hidden in the womb of the matter; this joining together must happen immediately at the beginning of the matter, so that the matter remains and persists.

Nature cannot do it alone, nor perform this Union <term>Conjunction</term>, because the action or doing <term>Actio</term> of Nature is contrary to the fire; and the Action of the fire is infinite <note>original: *infinita*; meaning it will continue to burn or consume without a natural stopping point</note>, and Nature, because she acts continuously, destroys what she has made.

The Artist <note>The alchemist is traditionally referred to as "the Artist," as alchemy was considered the "Great Art" (*Ars Magna*).</note> however, by joining them together, ensures that Nature, after a complete Action has occurred, ceases from her doing or Action.

Now the Artist is entirely finished and released from his procedure <term>Operation</term>, and therefore this Union <term>Conjunction</term> is quite an easy task.

<meta>Catchword: Task</meta>

<summary>This chapter explains that while Nature and fire drive the alchemical process, the alchemist (the Artist) must intervene to perform the Conjunction. This intervention ensures that the fire does not destroy the work and that the hidden Ferment can properly transform the matter.</summary>
<keywords>Conjunction, Ferment, Decoction, The Artist, Alchemy, Natural Action, Fire, Union of Matter</keywords>

The entire benefit and profit arises from the proper use of fire, according to the statement of Plato.

# Now follows a Practical Method in this Art, according to the Weights.

To compose the work, one should take one part of the **Body** <note>original: *Corporis*</note> of the **prepared Earth**, and four parts of the **Water of Heaven** <note>original: *Aquæ Cæli*</note>, and nothing else; much will remain behind during the **preparation**. One must add new water—which must also be prepared—as often as needed until it becomes like honey or curdled milk. Then, when it is fully **dissolved** <note>original: *resolviret*</note>, set it aside so that it may pass through the correct channels, either through a hare-skin <note>Used as a fine filter for delicate substances</note> or a double-layered cloth.

Afterwards, when all this is done, one must cleanse the **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurium*</note> with common salt and the strongest boiled vinegar for one hour; then it is drawn over the **helm** <term>alembic</term> <note>The "helm" is the cap of a distilling apparatus; "drawing over" refers to distillation</note> and washed with common (fresh) water so that the salt is removed. This washing with water may be repeated three or four times; and then the Mercury is ready to be made into an **amalgam**.

Then place your entire **composition** into a round glass vessel <note>original: *urinali rotundo*</note>, sealed with the **mud of wisdom** <term>luto sapientiæ</term> <note>A specialized airtight sealant made of clay, horse dung, and other binders used to protect the vessel from breaking and to keep it hermetically sealed</note>. Place it in **horse manure** <note>Commonly used in alchemy as a source of steady, gentle, and natural heat</note>, as is the custom, for the duration of one **philosophical month** <note>Typically forty days</note>, to **dissolve** <note>original: *solviren*</note> and to **rot** <note>original: *putresciren*; the process of breakdown before transformation</note>. When this has occurred, place it into another glass vessel with the **Seal of Hermes** <term>sigillo Hermetis</term> <note>A permanent glass-to-glass seal made by melting the neck of the flask shut</note>, and give it **fire in the third degree** <note>A specific intensity of heat, usually stronger than a water bath but less than a direct forge-fire</note>; thus it is accomplished.

### Now follows: In what amount of time one can learn this Art, according to the opinion of Morienus, a Roman Philosopher.

Morienus the Roman <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist credited with teaching the Art to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says: that the entire operation of the **Philosophers' Stone** <note>original: *Lapidis Philosophorum*</note>—namely, this heavenly, true, and correct Art—can be taught and learned within a single day, indeed in one hour, without greatly **exhausting** <term>overworking</term> <note>original: *defatigire*</note> one's body, as occurs in many other sciences; provided, however, that one has a good and sincere teacher, etc.

However, we are not speaking of someone who knows absolutely nothing of nature, possesses no **principles** <term>foundational laws</term> <note>original: *Principia*</note>, understands no **terminology** <note>original: *Terminum*</note>, and knows nothing of minerals, vegetables, and animals, the elements, etc. Rather, he must first learn to understand these things, as well as their benefit and harm, their qualities, figures, and allegories in speech or writing, etc. <note>The author emphasizes that while the "secret" of the Stone is simple, it requires a deep prerequisite knowledge of the natural world and alchemical symbolism.</note>

### Now follows: Whether the observation of the stars contributes anything to this Art, and the knowledge of the planets according to Senior Major.

Senior Major <note>Likely referring to Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century alchemist known in the West as "Senior," whose works emphasized the correspondence between the cosmos and the laboratory</note> says: Whoever wishes to value the influence of the heavens and the **impressions** <note>original: *Impressionibus*</note> of the planets, signs, stones, and also the elements, **joins the active with the passive** <note>original: *conjungiret activa passivis*; a fundamental alchemical concept of uniting opposing forces to create a new substance</note>.

<page-num>125</page-num>
<header>of the Sages.</header>

Therefore, it is not strictly necessary to know the **impressions** <term>celestial imprints</term> <note>original: *Impressiones*</note>, effects, and influences of the heavens beforehand.

Rhasis <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and alchemist</note> and Haly <note>Likely Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer</note>, etc., say that it is useful. However, it is enough to dispose the matter in our Art in such a way, and to give it the proper form, so that the celestial nature may act upon the **prepared or disposed things** <note>original: *præparata sive disposita*</note>.

This happens now in time, in the limit, and in the tempered limit <note>original: *tempore, termino, & termino temperato*; referring to the specific windows of time and conditions required for natural processes</note>, as the excellent Plato says: "The sun and man generate a man," <note>A common medieval adaptation of Aristotle's *Physics* (II, 2), suggesting that while the sun provides the general heat for life, specific biological acts produce individuals</note> and yet many people do not know the course of the heavens, and nonetheless procreation occurs. Likewise, the **sowers** <note>The OCR reads *See-Männer* (sailors), but the context of sowing seeds in fields strongly suggests a transcription error for *Säemänner* (sowers).</note> who scatter the seed upon the fields seldom know anything about it, yet it grows and is multiplied.

The animals and **beasts** <term>irrational creatures</term> <note>original: *Bruta*</note> produce their own kind without knowing anything about the influence of the stars. Also, minerals are generated within the earth, as stated in the *Brief Articles* of Master Dominicus of Langres <note>Dominicus Lingonensis, a 13th-century philosopher and theologian</note>, a great philosopher.

Thus it is also with the **blessed Stone of the Philosophers** <note>original: *Lapis Philosophorum benedictus*</note>.

### We proceed further to a treatise which is called *THE LIGHT OF THE PHILOSOPHERS* <note>original: *LUMEN PHILOSOPHORUM*</note>.

### Here begins the treatise which is called a Light of all *Philosophers*, or a **Luminare** <term>a source of light or celestial body</term>.

->In the Name of the Most Holy Trinity.<-

It is to be known that our **Medicine** <term>the alchemical Elixir or Stone</term> shall be made from two things, namely, **from body and spirit** <note>original: *ex corpore & spiritu*</note>.

The **Bodies** <note>original: *Corpora*</note> are gold and silver—not the common ones, but ours. And it is necessary that it be from gold and silver. Gold is necessary if we wish to elevate <term>transmute into a higher state</term> lesser metals into gold; silver, however, if we make true silver from an imperfect **body**, because the **tincture** <term>the color-giving and transforming essence</term> of gold is in gold, and the tincture of silver is in silver.

For this reason, it is necessary that one of these metals be present in our tincture, either gold or silver.

Nature is not generated except from its own nature, just as a human comes from a human, a horse from a horse, and each generates its like.

A little **leaven** <note>The author uses the metaphor of sourdough (ferment) to explain how a small amount of the Alchemical Stone can transform a large mass of metal.</note> draws to its warm and moist nature a great quantity of the flour from which the said leaven was made.

Likewise, gold and silver are returned to the same form from which they originated—that is, into **quicksilver** <note>original: *Argentum vivum*</note>—according to their nature.

Now someone might say: if our **tincture** <term>the substance used to transform base metals</term> is indeed complete within gold and silver, why does it not immediately transform other base and corrupt metals?

To this it is answered: You well know that a small child consists of both body and soul just as much as a grown man, and yet it cannot perform those duties which a grown man performs until such a child also reaches his manly and perfect age; and nonetheless, such a small child proceeds step-by-step, from year to year, until he reaches his perfection.

Thus, to return to our analogy, gold and silver do not perform their work in our **Medicine** <term>the alchemical Elixir or Stone</term> unless they are changed from their coarse nature, and from their **corporeality** <note>their solid, physical state</note> to **spirituality** <note>a refined, volatile, or "living" state</note>. And for as long as it takes until they are transformed back to their true nature, they provide **tincture** <note>the power to color or change</note> and **augmentation** <note>the ability to increase in power or quantity</note> through heat and moisture.

The **Spirit** <note>the volatile or gaseous principle of a substance</note> is necessary in our Medicine because we have said that our Medicine must be of a hot (fiery) nature, and thus of a very subtle nature—namely, the nature of the **Quintessence** <note>original: *Quintæ Essentiæ*; the purest, "fifth" essence above the four elements</note>—because the metals are coarse and heavy; thus, in a common way, from such a nature of theirs, no sub- <note>The text cuts off here, likely intending to say "no subtle substance can be made."</note>

## Concerning the Fixation of the Body & Spirit.

When, therefore, out of the **Body & Spirit** <note>original: *ex Corpore & Spiritu*</note>, one thing has been made, we must then make that same essence a **fixed Body & Spirit** <note>original: *Corpus & Spiritum fixum*</note> such that it may be a pure **Body** <term>original: *Corpus*</term> acting **as a mover** <note>original: *ut movens*</note>, resisting the fire.

Note well why our Medicine transforms other lesser and corrupt metals into gold and silver, since the Medicine is itself made from gold or silver.

## ANDREAS OSIANDER.

Now follows a small treatise by **ANDREAS OSIANDER**, an excellent philosopher in this art <note>The "art" refers to alchemy, often called the "Hermetic Art."</note>.

Among the secret philosophical studies, one must particularly consider and commit to memory that mystery: namely, how to turn all metals into gold. However, one must not approach such a work with unwashed hands <note>A common idiomatic expression (from the Latin *illotis manibus*) meaning to approach a sacred or complex task without proper preparation or purity of intent.</note>, but with prayer, sound reason, and a prudent moderation of the labor.

Many have indeed doubted, and many still doubt the truth of this work, but they do so wrongly and imprudently <note>original Latin: *sed insipienter*, meaning "but foolishly."</note>.

In this work, there is not only one single way, yet there is surely one and the same purpose.

When the **dissolution** <note>original: *Dissolution*</note> has completely occurred, place (fit) a helm <note>a distillation cap or "alembic" used to collect vapors</note> over the glass containing the matter, and put it in the furnace to distill.

Then there appears and rises up the **Star of May Dew** <note>original: *Stella Roris Maji*</note>, the **Water of Life** <note>original: *Aqva vitæ*</note>, the **Tear of the Eye** <note>original: *Lacryma oculi*</note>, the **Virgin’s Milk** <note>original: *Lac Virginis*</note>, the **purest matter of the stone** <note>original: *purissima materia lapidis*</note>.

In the final perfect **preparation** <note>original: *Præparation*</note> it is bitter **with respect to Silver** <note>original: *ad Lunam*; literally "to the Moon," the alchemical symbol for silver</note>, a **sour earth** <note>original: *Terra acetosa*</note>, volatile, and not **fixed** <note>original: *fix*; "fixed" substances are stable under heat and do not evaporate</note>.

It is incorruptible or bodiless <note>original: *incorporalis*</note>, **almost reduced to powder through digestion...** <note>original: *fere per digestionem in pulverem redu-*</note>

# Of the Blessed Stone

Take those remaining residues <note>original: *feces*; the solid dregs or sediment left over after a chemical process</note>, and place them into digestion <term>Digestion</term> <note>the process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat to mature or soften it</note> in a dry heat <note>original: *stupha sicca*; literally a "dry stove," providing an environment of hot air</note>, just as you did before; afterward, place it in a water bath <note>original: *Balneum Mariæ*; a "Mary's Bath" or double-boiler used for gentle, indirect heating</note> so that it may dissolve <note>original: *dissolvire*</note>. Next, place the matter in warm ashes, but first with a gentle fire, in a sublimation vessel <note>original: *Vas sublimationis*; a glass container designed so that heated solids vaporize and then reform as a purified crust at the top</note>, and shortly thereafter give it a very strong fire; then, an elemental fire <note>original: *Ignis elementaris*</note> will rise up the sides of the glass like a liquid <note>original: *Liqvor*</note> of a very red oil. Such a **method** <note>original: *Modus*</note> is stronger for the Redness, but weaker for the Whiteness.

# Of the Blessed Stone

[fully] accomplished is well known; therefore, in our work, Art is nothing other than an <term>assistant</term> <note>original: *Adjuvamen*; a helper or auxiliary force.</note>, an aid and a helping hand to Nature. This is clearly seen among common people, artists, and craftsmen in various—indeed, very many—arts and trades.

For example: Nature produces and generates wood, from which many kinds of things are made and crafted, both coarse and refined. Indeed, to go further, wood is burned to ash; the burning creates ash, and from that ash, glass is mostly made through Art—glass which is bright, beautiful, and clear, even though the ash itself is black, gray, and ugly.

Thus it is to be understood that if the <term>first matter</term> <note>original: *prima materia*; the fundamental, formless substance that alchemists believed resided within all objects.</note> of glass had not been present in the ash—indeed, in the wood itself—then the hidden Art could by no means have produced the glass, nor could it have brought it forth and completed it without Nature <note>original: *sine Natura philosophica*; "without philosophical nature," meaning without following the natural laws discovered by the sages.</note>.

Consider then, that nothing can be brought out of a thing which is not already within it.

Therefore, it remains so: Nature and Art must be and stand together, and only then do they yield benefit and fruit. Every seed gives the fruit which Nature assigns to it; however, the farmer or the master of the house must possess art, knowledge, understanding, and labor.

# Of the Blessed Stone

...other beings might be produced, other than from the aforementioned two bodies, by means of their nature.

Many, however, do not wish to believe this; I wish, then, that they would investigate the matter more thoroughly to arrive at the right path.

A philosopher says that, indeed, in every perfect body, its **Sulphur** <term>Sulphur: in alchemy, the active, combustible principle representing the "soul" or "form" of a substance</term> and **Mercury** <term>Mercury: the fluid, volatile principle representing the "spirit" or "matter"</term> are contained, yet in one more ripe and pure than in another—**this is the Sulphur of the Philosophers** <note>original: *hoc est Sulphur Philosphorum*</note>. For example:

That a redness is found in gold comes from the fact that it is more **digested** <term>digestion: the process of maturing or ripening a substance through gentle, consistent heat, similar to how the body processes food</term> than other metals; and that silver is white is because it is less digested than gold.

Accordingly, it follows that one should follow nature through **Art** <note>In this context, "Art" refers to the alchemist's skill and laboratory practice used to replicate and accelerate natural processes</note> by cooking, boiling, digesting, maturing, refining, etc., all of which are **in practice** <note>original: *in Actu*</note> the same thing.

Nature holds within itself a natural fire; thus, the artist of nature must also follow nature with fire and heat in the Art.

In silver, there is a **simple sulphur** <note>original: *Sulphur simplex*</note> which is not as digested as that in gold; it naturally holds a fire within itself and acts **secretly** <note>original: *occultè*</note>, both in nature and in Art.

It is not impossible that Art, by means of nature, can reach higher and higher; and what nature must often accomplish through a great length of time, Art does—if the artist hits upon the right method—in a shorter time...

# Of the Wise
->M 2<-

...time, for by itself Nature can do nothing in our Work <note>The "Work" or *Opus* refers to the Great Work of alchemy: the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> if it is not aided by a skillful hand; however, few good **workers** <term>workers: translated from *Laboratores*, referring to practical alchemists who work at the furnace</term> are found.

Thus, other **metals** <note>original: *Metalla*</note> do not become gold if they are not also processed through a good **digestion** <term>digestion: the alchemical process of maturing or ripening a substance through gentle, consistent heat, mimicking the Earth's natural processes</term>. But simple **laborants** <note>original: *Laboranten*; a term often used to describe unlearned practitioners or "puffers" who lack philosophical understanding</note> do not understand this, as they cannot grasp it correctly; and while they think they want to make something better out of a base thing, they instead make a worse and baser thing out of a better essence.

They seek gold and silver in **excrement** <note>original: *stercoribus*</note>, in muck and filth, and in combustible things, from which they nevertheless do not obtain the **Sulfur** and **Mercury** <note>Sulfur and Mercury were considered the two primary "seeds" or principles from which all metals are formed.</note>. In gold and silver are **tinting** <term>tinting: from *tingirende*, the power of a perfected substance to project its quality and color onto a base metal, transforming it into gold or silver</term> rays, and these metals are those which are well **digested** and **matured**, though gold is better than silver.

But the **Art** <note>In this context, "Art" refers to the skill and technology of alchemy</note> is worth nothing without **Nature**, which the Art must follow; thus it remains: Nature and Art must stand together. Therefore, there is no need for so much speaking and writing, because experience confirms it.

The **imperfect metals** <note>Imperfect metals usually refer to lead, tin, iron, and copper, which were seen as "diseased" or immature versions of gold.</note> must be treated and purified with the **minor minerals**, and once they are purified, **Digestion**, **Maturation**, etc., must follow, as has already been mentioned above.

From this it is clear that the **minor minerals** <note>original: *minora Mineralia*; secondary substances like salts, vitriols, or antimony used to refine metals</note> cannot **tint**, unless they are first combined with gold and silver.

Therefore, nothing can be **tinted** <term>tinted: from the Latin *tingere*, meaning to transform the color and nature of a base metal into gold or silver</term> except by those things in which the **Tincture** <note>The "Tincture" is the active, transformative essence of the Philosopher's Stone that "colors" or transmutes base metals.</note> is already hidden; otherwise, time and labor are lost.
